chapter: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
title: Racial mixing in the Goodman band compared with Jackie Robinson
summary: Wilson says the band treated him like family, audiences were enthusiastic, and the experience was entirely different from Robinson's ten years later.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I might have. I can't really recall it right now. But I'll tell you what, I'd like to get, while we're on this subject of the band and the movie, I'd like to just find out, how was it playing with the guys? You know, you
Oh, yeah, wonderfully. You mean as far as the race thing?

Oh, it was a tremendous success. As a matter of fact, it was an asset, racial mixing. The interest in the United States was tremendous, and the public was so for the thing that not one negative voice in any audience did we ever get. Just tremendous enthusiasm. This interracial thing was just wonderful.
But in the band, was there any incident, like maybe one guy, second trombone player or first trombone player might have -- like Jackie Robinson had a problem.
Completely different from Jackie's -- Jackie had tremendous problems with baseball players.

Oh, no, the cooperation was good in the band. We were like brothers, the whole outfit. Because everybody knew what was happening, you know. And the Goodman Band, the band was composed of -- there were Southerners in it, Harry James from Texas and Dave Mathews from Oklahoma, and there were Jews and Christians and Lionel Hampton and I represented

the Negro in the band. And Goodman was Jewish, and some of the guys were Italians. And Ziggy Elman, I think, was Jewish background. But the thing was as solid as a family, the Goodman thing. We were all there, just like brothers.

And we were all very much aware of what was going on, too. Everybody was a dedicated musician, we believed in what we were doing, socially and musically. But it was very different from Jackie Robinson having to fight guys on the team and the fans and so on, insulting players on the field, giving them a hard time. The jazz fans were like they were just hungry for this sort of thing.
Yeah, ten years prior to breaking the color line in sports.
